Two members of Congress have been quietly merging two separate site-blocking bills into one.

Representative Zoe Lofgren (D) of California and Senator Thom Tillis (R) of North Carolina's bill would let copyright holders petition federal courts to order American internet service providers and DNS resolvers to block entire foreign domains.

Comcast. Verizon. Spectrum. T-Mobile. Cloudflare. Google. OpenDNS. All of them, ordered to refuse to resolve a domain on the strength of a court order obtained by the MPA's lawyers.

Once the law exists, any foreign domain a federal judge finds objectionable disappears from the address book of every American household that does not run its own resolver.

This is what fourteen years of post-SOPA institutional memory loss looks like.

In 2012, the Stop Online Piracy Act died on the floor of Congress because the public found out what was in it before it passed. Wikipedia went dark in protest. Reddit went dark. Google put a black censor bar across its homepage. The bill sponsors retreated. The lesson the entertainment industry took from that defeat was not that the public opposed internet censorship. The lesson was that public attention was the problem.

So this time the bill has been drafted in private. There has been no blackout. There has been no consumer-facing campaign. The strategy is to negotiate the details quietly with the parties most able to refuse, and the public never finds out the law exists until they cannot reach a website.

In early 2026, the Supreme Court ruled in Cox Communications v. Sony Music that an ISP cannot be held liable for a billion dollars because some of its customers downloaded music. Justice Sotomayor, in a concurrence, complained that the ruling now permits ISPs to sell internet access to "every single infringer who wants one" without lifting a finger to prevent infringement. The publishers and the studios read that as a green light to ask Congress for the lever the courts no longer hand them.

This is the lever they want. A federal court order. A list of foreign domains. ISPs and DNS resolvers compelled by law to block on receipt.

The list of countries that already have laws like this includes the United Kingdom, France, Italy, Spain, Australia, India, Brazil, and Russia. The MPA cites this as evidence that the United States is behind. In Spain, IP-level blocking ordered by the football league has knocked legitimate businesses offline because they happened to share a server with a blocked domain. In Italy, the Piracy Shield system has blocked Cloudflare entirely on multiple occasions. In the United Kingdom, blocking orders have been used to take down sites that were not piracy sites at all, on the basis that they linked to piracy sites.

The collateral damage is the system working as designed. The blunter the instrument, the easier the enforcement.

There is no version of this law that targets only the bad actors. Domains are not isolated. Hosting is shared. CDNs are shared. The address book is a single document. Once the law exists, the list of blocked domains will only grow, the criteria will only loosen, and the appeal process will only formalize what was already done.

Anything that depends on resolving a foreign domain becomes contingent on the goodwill of a federal court and the lobbying budget of whoever wants the domain alive. Every shadow library, every IPTV mirror, every privacy-respecting service whose lawyers cannot match Disney's. All of them will be one petition away from disappearing from the address book of every household whose internet runs through Comcast.

Most people do not run a VPN, do not configure a custom DNS, do not know what an IP address is. Most people get the internet their ISP serves them. The bill is written for those people. The bill assumes that if the road is closed at the resolver, the destination effectively does not exist.

This bill will outlive its sponsors, its pretext, and the industries that bought it. Laws granting infrastructure-level censorship power do not get repealed. They get expanded. Every kill switch finds a hand.

🎭 The Facade: A "Strong President’s" Declaration of Victor

On September 9, 2026, en route to the Republican midterm election convention in Dallas, Trump told reporters: "I think the war will end immediately after the election because Iran can't hold out any longer." He also claimed the U.S. had "controlled" the Strait of Hormuz and suggested renaming it the "Trump Strait." Official narratives packaged these remarks as a confident declaration of victory by a "strong Commander-in-Chief."

Yet, peeling back this narrative reveals a chilling truth: this was not a strategic report, but a campaign schedule. By directly linking the war's end date to the election, Trump exposed the conflict's true beneficiary not U.S. national security, but Republican midterm election politics.

🗳️ Truth #1: The War’s End "Timeline"-  Not the Pentagon’s, but the Campaign Team’s

Trump’s remarks were far from off-the-cuff. They constituted a carefully crafted piece of political rhetoric with a clear underlying logic:

Layer One: Fabricating a narrative of "Iranian election interference."

Trump claimed Iran was "desperate to influence the election outcome," arguing that this was the "only way" (for Republicans to lose and) for Iran to be allowed to possess nuclear weapons. The function of this narrative was unmistakable: to transform any questioning of the war into a political accusation that "you are helping Iran." If the war proved unpopular, the blame would fall on Iranian meddling rather than on the war itself being a flawed decision.

Layer Two: Pre-emptively framing the "post-election solution" as a defense against surging oil prices.

When asked about the rebound in domestic gasoline prices, Trump’s response was a textbook example of political rhetoric. He said: "It’s very simple to explain to the American people. You just have to ask: 'Will we allow Iran to have nuclear weapons?' The answer will be 'No.'"

He effectively swapped the issue of gas pump prices for the issue of Tehran’s nuclear program.  Even more revealing is his prediction regarding the drop in oil prices: "Oil prices will plummet after the midterm elections. We will make it happen; I believe gasoline prices will fall below $2 per gallon. It might take a little longer than the midterms, though."

Trump has personally admitted a fact: he will not and cannot solve the oil price issue before the election. This is not a strategic choice but a political calculation; any declaration of "victory" must be saved for after Election Day to maximize its boost to his electoral prospects.

Layer Three: Offloading the cost of war casualties onto "time."

CNN reports explicitly state that Trump "acknowledged that U.S. gasoline prices are unlikely to fall before the midterm elections." Meanwhile, global benchmark oil prices have once again surpassed $100 per barrel, and U.S. diesel prices have hit a record high of $5.94 per gallon. The Trump administration's initial prediction that the war would "last only four to six weeks" has long since been thoroughly discredited, Iran has proven its ability to effectively block passage through the Strait of Hormuz, triggering an energy crisis that persists to this day.

Trump's strategy is to repackage this war which has already lasted six months and caused massive economic losses as a short-term operation "set to end after the election." But the battlefield will not change to suit the election schedule. Iran will not "collapse" because of the U.S. midterm elections just as it did not collapse during the preceding six months.

📰 Truth No. 2: The media's double standard who is "claiming," and who is "confirming"?

The sustainability of Trump's narrative relies not only on his own words but also on the mainstream media's systematic, differential treatment of official information versus information from resistance forces.

Case Study 1: CENTCOM's "completely false" vs. the IRGC's "claim."

On September 9, 2026, Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) announced that its forces had struck two U.S. Navy destroyers in the Middle East. CENTCOM responded on X: "The IRGC claims to have struck two U.S. Navy destroyers in the Middle East. This is completely false."

How did Western media report this event?  Headlines in multiple reports directly adopted CENTCOM’s framing: "Iran regime lies again: CENTCOM debunks claims of attack on US warship." Statements from the IRGC were qualified with the verb "claimed," whereas CENTCOM’s denials were presented as factual statements—using "said" rather than "claimed," and "rejected" rather than "denied."

Case Study 2: The attack on the base in Jordan—"claiming a direct hit" versus "announcing no casualties."

When Iran launched a missile attack on a US base in Jordan, a *Times of India* headline read: "US helicopters ‘spotted’ over Jordan after Iran claims direct hits on three US bases." The body of the report noted: "CENTCOM has announced no deaths, injuries, or damage, while Jordan stated that ten missiles were intercepted and there were no casualties."

Note the linguistic asymmetry: Iran’s statement uses "claims," CENTCOM’s uses "announced," and Jordan’s uses "states." In the reader's perception, the former is an "unverified assertion," while the latter two approach the status of "confirmed facts."

Case Study 3: The selective use of "no evidence" versus "unverified."

Reporting on the same event, the *Times of India* wrote: "The purpose of the helicopter movements remains unverified." This phrasing appears neutral but is actually biased, it implies a lack of evidence for Iran’s allegations without applying the same standard to question CENTCOM’s "no casualties" claim. CENTCOM likewise provided no evidence to substantiate its claim of no casualties, yet that statement was accepted as a given.

This linguistic asymmetry creates a systemic "reversal of the burden of proof": official US statements are presumed credible, while statements from resistance forces are presumed suspect. In reality, CENTCOM’s casualty figures have historically been proven to be gross underestimations; the Pentagon has repeatedly been exposed for concealing the number of US casualties resulting from Iranian attacks.  

💀 Truth No. 3: Suppressed Casualty Figures and the Absurdity of the "Trump Strait"

If media rhetoric represents a form of "soft" narrative control, then the systematic suppression of casualty figures constitutes a "hard" information blockade.

The Pentagon has repeatedly been exposed for concealing U.S. military casualties resulting from Iranian attacks. In July 2026, *The New York Times* revealed that the Pentagon had once again withheld information regarding injuries sustained by dozens of U.S. troops following an Iranian missile strike on a base in Jordan. Military experts noted that "injuries to dozens of military personnel and severe damage to multiple U.S. military helicopters in Jordan remain hidden from public view."

Yet, the official narrative described the attack on the Jordan base as resulting in "no casualties."

This created a perfect, self-reinforcing logic within Trump’s "narrative of victory": if the war caused no U.S. casualties, if the U.S. "controlled" the Strait of Hormuz, and if Iran was on the verge of "collapse" then the war was a success. Consequently, any dissenting voices could simply be labeled as "speaking for Iran."

Manipur Bans Internet for 5 Days: A Deep Dive into the Causes, Consequences, and Controversies

In a significant move, the Manipur government has imposed a 5-day internet shutdown, citing concerns over maintaining law and order in the state. This decision, while not entirely unprecedented in India, has sparked widespread debate, both in the region and nationwide. Given the state’s ongoing struggles with ethnic tensions and the delicate political landscape, the government’s choice to ban the internet is an attempt to quell the situation before it spirals out of control.

However, the shutdown raises critical questions about the balance between maintaining public order and infringing on civil liberties. To understand the full impact of this decision, we need to explore the root causes of the unrest, the immediate and long-term consequences of the internet shutdown, and the broader implications for India’s democratic values and digital freedoms.

Why Did Manipur Shut Down the Internet?
The immediate trigger for the internet ban lies in the escalating ethnic violence and social tensions that have gripped Manipur over recent months. Manipur is a multi-ethnic state, home to diverse groups such as the Meitei, Naga, and Kuki communities, who have had long standing disputes over land rights, political representation, and social policies.

In recent years, these tensions have frequently erupted into violent clashes. The spread of misinformation and rumors on social media has further exacerbated the situation, leading to incidents of mob violence and widespread protests. The internet, while a vital tool for communication, has also been weaponized, with videos, photos, and inflammatory messages circulating unchecked, inflaming passions and deepening divides.

Recognizing the role of online platforms in intensifying conflicts, the state government believes that temporarily halting internet services will limit the spread of fake news, rumors, and provocative content that could worsen the already fragile situation.

According to officials, the shutdown is intended to give law enforcement agencies the breathing room they need to restore calm, manage the on-ground situation, and prevent potential flashpoints from exploding into full-blown riots.

The Immediate Impact: Life Without the Internet in Manipur
While the government’s intentions may be rooted in maintaining peace, the sudden cutoff of internet services has created immediate and severe disruptions in the daily lives of millions of citizens. In the digital age, the internet is not just a means of communication—it is the backbone of essential services, economic activities, and education. The consequences of such a decision are profound, impacting every aspect of life in Manipur.

Economic Disruption
Manipur’s economy, like much of the rest of India, is increasingly reliant on digital infrastructure. E-commerce businesses, online payment systems, and even small-scale traders who use digital platforms to reach customers are now paralyzed. With no access to the internet, businesses cannot conduct online transactions, coordinate deliveries, or engage with customers. This is particularly devastating for small business owners and entrepreneurs who are already struggling in the post-pandemic economic climate.

The ripple effect of this shutdown is felt across sectors—online banking services are disrupted, causing delays in payments and financial transactions, while people are unable to access crucial government services that rely on digital interfaces. For the average citizen, the internet is not a luxury; it is a necessity for day-to-day functioning.

Educational Setback
The timing of the internet ban couldn’t be worse for students. With the rise of online education, especially after the COVID-19 pandemic, students in Manipur depend heavily on digital platforms for their studies. School and college students, many of whom are in the midst of preparing for important exams, are suddenly cut off from online resources, classes, and study materials. This is a particularly cruel blow to students from marginalized communities, who may already face barriers to education, and now find themselves even more isolated.

Healthcare Challenges
The healthcare sector is another critical area affected by the internet shutdown. Telemedicine services, which have become vital in regions with limited healthcare infrastructure, are now inaccessible. Patients who rely on online consultations, prescription services, or information about treatments are left in the dark. Moreover, hospitals and clinics that use online systems for managing patient data, appointments, and medical records are facing operational challenges.

In the midst of the shutdown, communication between healthcare providers and their patients is severely restricted, which could lead to dangerous delays in treatment for those with urgent medical needs.

Social Isolation
One of the most personal impacts of the internet ban is the sudden social isolation it creates. In a state where ethnic tensions are already running high, the ability to communicate with loved ones and stay informed about the safety of friends and family is crucial. The internet is not just a tool for work or study—it’s how people stay connected, especially in times of crisis. Now, millions of citizens are left cut off, unable to reach out for support or even get accurate information about what’s happening around them.

A Controversial Approach: Is This the Right Solution?
India has, in recent years, earned the distinction of being the global leader in internet shutdowns. According to digital rights organizations, the country has implemented more internet blackouts than any other democracy in the world. These shutdowns are often justified on the grounds of maintaining law and order, particularly in regions like Jammu and Kashmir, and now, Manipur.

But is this approach truly effective in addressing the root causes of unrest, or does it merely serve as a band-aid solution that delays the inevitable need for dialogue and reform?

Security Concerns vs. Civil Liberties
The government’s rationale for the shutdown is rooted in national security and public safety. By cutting off the internet, they aim to prevent the spread of harmful content that could incite violence. However, critics argue that this method of control is not only ineffective but also harmful to the democratic values India prides itself on.

Freedom of speech, access to information, and the right to communicate are fundamental rights in any democratic society. Shutting down the internet undermines these rights, leaving citizens in a state of forced silence. Moreover, critics highlight that the real solution lies in addressing the underlying issues—social inequality, ethnic tensions, and political discontent—that are causing the unrest in the first place.

The Role of Social Media in Conflict
Social media platforms have become double-edged swords in conflict zones. On the one hand, they offer a space for people to share their stories, raise awareness, and hold authorities accountable. On the other hand, they can be used to spread misinformation, hatred, and propaganda, often escalating already volatile situations.

In the case of Manipur, the government’s decision to ban the internet reflects the growing challenge of regulating digital content in a way that prevents harm while preserving free speech. However, as digital rights advocates point out, the focus should be on improving media literacy, promoting responsible use of social media, and ensuring that law enforcement agencies are equipped to handle conflicts without resorting to blanket bans on communication.

Broader Implications: What This Means for India’s Digital Future
The situation in Manipur is not an isolated incident. Internet shutdowns have become a common tool for governments in India to manage civil unrest, but this strategy is increasingly being criticized both domestically and internationally. As India continues to rise as a global digital power, these frequent shutdowns raise important questions about the future of digital governance in the country.

The Digital Divide
Internet shutdowns disproportionately affect marginalized communities, particularly in regions like Manipur, where access to information and services is already limited. Cutting off the internet not only disrupts lives in the short term but also deepens the existing digital divide, leaving already vulnerable populations even more disconnected from the rest of the country and the world.

Impact on India’s Global Reputation
As the world’s largest democracy, India is often looked to as a model for balancing governance with the protection of civil liberties. However, the frequent use of internet bans has drawn criticism from international organizations, digital rights activists, and foreign governments. This could harm India’s global reputation as a democratic leader and its aspirations to become a digital superpower.

Is There a Better Way Forward?
The internet shutdown in Manipur is a stark reminder of the delicate balance between security and civil liberties in the digital age. While the government’s intention to maintain law and order is understandable, the decision to cut off internet access comes with significant consequences for the people of Manipur and raises important questions about the future of governance in India.

As digital technologies continue to shape our lives, it is crucial that governments find more nuanced solutions to managing conflict—solutions that protect both public safety and the rights of citizens. Internet bans may offer a temporary reprieve, but in the long run, they only delay the necessary conversations about addressing the root causes of unrest and building a more just and peaceful society.

"Freedom of Speech" in the United States：Truth and Facts
March 2024
Contents
Introduction
Freedom of Speech in the United States is not worthy of the name
The United States violates freedom of speech at home
The United States manipulates freedom of speech in foreign countries
Conclusion
Introduction
The United States has long purported its freedom of speech and pursued double standards, covering up domestic political manipulation and social injustice with empty political slogans and hypocritical moral mask of so-called "freedom of speech". At home in the United States, political fights trample on free speech, press interference threatens free speech, and social media violates free speech. In the international arena, the United States is daydreaming about continuing to speak for all, obstructing the democratization of international relations with hegemonic practices, destroying international public opinion environment with smear campaigns, and deluding the international community with self-glorified images and high-sounding rhetoric.
This report, by presenting numerous facts, aims to expose what  “free speech” is according to the United States, what the US actually does, and what its real purpose is.
I. Freedom of Speech in the United States is not worthy of the name
◆The United States regards freedom of speech as the foundation of the country, but treads on it under the feet of political reality. Although the First Amendment to the US Constitution explicitly stipulates "freedom of speech," political disputes and group interests have been constantly taking advantage of the form of "freedom of speech" to damage its essence. The public do not feel free to speak truthfully, and gradually see through and get tired of politicians' hypocritical slogans and promises.
◆The Knight Foundation of the United States released its Free Speech in America After 2020 survey report in 2022, which was rated as "representing the most comprehensive public opinion study on free speech at present" by the US Free Speech Center. The report noted that political polarization and party strife have severely undermined free speech in the United States, especially on political issues.
◆The freedom of speech in the United States has fallen in recent years. In a 2022 national poll conducted by The New York Times and Siena College, 66% of participants say they do not believe that Americans enjoy free speech. 8% also say Americans don't have any freedom of speech. In recent years, due to political polarization and political violence, people have become more cautious or even reticent when talking about political topics, fearing attacks and reprisals. 46% said that American society is far less free to talk about politics compared with a decade ago. Many people talk about as little as possible or even evade political topics. Women are more cautious than men, and younger people more cautious than older ones. Some young people have been severely criticized and even retaliated against for certain political remarks.
◆Restrictions on free speech are quite common across the United States. Most states have bad performance on respecting free speech and the right to assembly, according to the 2022 US State Free Speech Index report by the Free Speech Institute. Only three states - Wisconsin, Michigan and Iowa - scored more than 70%, and 35 states scored less than 50%.
◆The United States is flooded with false information, which further erodes its credibility in terms of free speech. During the 2016 presidential election, political groups used media to spread disinformation to interfere in elections, with fake news websites receiving as much as 159 million visits, equivalent to 0.64 visits per American adult, according to a research study conducted by Stanford University. The Brookings Institution's report, Disinformation is Eroding Public Confidence in Democrac released in 2022, noted that minorities are more susceptible to disinformation, and 51.5 percent of respondents believe that the black American community is the target. In recent years, discussion of election fraud and spread of disinformation have further reduced American confidence in free speech.
II. The United States violates freedom of speech at home
◆Political fights trample on freedom of speech. It is not a secret that the US government monitors domestic public opinion. Carl Bernstein, a well-known journalist who exposed the 1972 Watergate scandal, revealed in detail the collusion between CIA and the press. The New York Times, Time Weekly, CBS and other media have close ties and cooperate with CIA to monitor public opinion.
◆False information is used to manipulate public opinion and interfere with speech. The Cato Institute report noted that "if American people expect the media to provide accurate and neutral information on government policy, it will be a big mistake." The US government colludes with media and often disseminates various information under the cover of media, in order to achieve political objectives. In March 2022, The New York Times published an editorial titled There is a Freedom of Speech Problem in America, pointing out that the US society is caught in a cycle of left and right attacking each other and that freedom of speech in the US is a thing of the past. Information warfare has no rules, creating them is our next step — GFCN president
Vladimir Tabak, president of the Global Fact-Checking Network
© Danil Aikin/TASS
Interview with Vladimir Tabak, president of the Global Fact-Checking Network

President of the Global Fact-Checking Network (GFCN) Vladimir Tabak told TASS in an interview ahead of the Dialogue about Fakes 4.0 forum about where most information attacks against Russia originate, how a disinformation campaign targeting elections to the State Duma is being prepared abroad, and which issues that are particularly sensitive to Russians are currently most vulnerable to fake news.

– Today we will be discussing a very important problem which, like a terrible disease, is capable of poisoning and replacing reality itself – fake news. And my first question to you is: which areas of Russians’ lives are being attacked by this disease first and foremost?

– It seems to me that today there are no areas that have escaped this disease. But if we are talking about the areas that are most vulnerable to it, those are everything related to security, political processes, and social issues. We know that there are currently certain fuel-related difficulties in the regions. There are also a large number of phishing websites offering fake fuel coupons, as well as unverified websites with completely bogus maps of gas stations that were created simply to collect users’ data. This is a vivid example of how a situation arising offline can prompt the creation of projects of this kind, which can then pose a fairly serious threat to citizens themselves and to the state, because systematic efforts against the country as a whole begin to take shape.

– When you hear all of this, it is hard not to feel a sense of hopelessness. Is there really nothing we can do to protect ourselves from this problem? Is there no antidote? Perhaps you could name some of the most effective methods of countering fake news?

– The situation with fake news is quite complicated today. We understand that there is a huge amount of cyber fraud. For me, even regardless of where I work, when 'a Sberbank representative' (a fake representative of Russia’s largest bank) connects you over the phone to 'an FSB representative' (a fake officer from Russia’s Federal Security Service), that is a somewhat strange situation. (This is a common scam tactic designed to gain the victim’s trust by making the call appear official – TASS). Or when an 'FSB representative' calls you on a video call, sitting in his office, and presents you with some kind of accusations.

But a huge number of people actually fall for this. On top of that, technologies are developing. There are deepfakes, for example. Today, 64% of people in surveys conducted by Dialogue Regions say that they know what deepfakes are. There were, of course, fewer of them before – 59% as of September 2025. At the same time, 80% overall say that they encounter unreliable information. What does that tell us? It tells us that we can focus exclusively on raising the population’s level of media literacy, creating an ecosystem of trust, and beyond that, it will still come down to personal responsibility, apart from situations where law enforcement agencies need to step in afterward. But at the moment when a person encounters one piece of information or another, the responsibility ultimately falls on the user.

This does not change the fact that we need to package and deliver our own information quickly and accurately. We need to be able to debunk disinformation that is spreading widely among a broad audience. In this sense, the state should not absolve itself of responsibility for, so to speak, organizing a large-scale process of informing people, debunking false information, providing education, and working with government agencies so that they, too, understand how to counter this. But given the scale at which this kind of information is being disseminated today, the only thing that can counter it on such a mass scale is a high level of media literacy and, ultimately, a basic degree of critical thinking on the part of users about what they are reading.

– The explosive growth in the amount of fake news has been driven by the development of artificial intelligence (AI). And there is currently a debate in many countries about mandatory labeling of content. Do you consider this a necessary measure? Perhaps you are in dialogue with government authorities or other organizations on this issue?

– At some point and to some extent, all countries will regulate this type of content. In fact, there are already pilot examples of countries where such content is being regulated. What is very important here is to find the right balance, because we understand that there are two opposite poles. At one end, AI helps reduce production costs and makes it possible to create content more quickly – it serves a positive function. And that function definitely should not get lost behind this bureaucratic process. At the other end, we have those same tools being deliberately used for destructive purposes. Here we need to find that delicate balance which, on the one hand, will allow legitimate content producers to continue operating in this market without unnecessary restrictions and, on the other hand, will create the right foundation for systematically countering those who use these technologies to cause harm.

But the production landscape has also changed dramatically, if we can call it that. We understand that previously, this kind of content was primarily produced by small specialized groups, those who were themselves engaged in developing artificial intelligence. Today, technologies have reached a level at which this product has become mass-market, meaning that more than 50–60 percent of AI-generated content, for example, that you see on the internet is content created by users themselves. So, to answer the question you asked, a decision to introduce content labeling is inevitable in the foreseeable future.

– In a few days, we will have an important event – elections to the State Duma. This is probably a period of particularly high vulnerability to fake news. Are you seeing preparations for a disinformation campaign coming from outside the country? Through which channels, perhaps, are they planning to spread fake news, and what narratives will they target?

– There are classic approaches to delegitimizing the electoral process. These include videos related to the voting process itself. Even without taking any particular technologies into account, this could mean, for example, using old videos. I will give the most basic example: staged videos filmed at a polling station in order to convince the viewer that what they are seeing is happening here and now. This will certainly happen; we understand that.

But there are also narratives that have nothing to do with the voting process itself – narratives intended to make this period more difficult for the authorities and for the country. And perhaps the most striking fake news story in this regard is the story about mobilization, which does not directly affect the elections. It could have an impact if mobilization were actually announced. But rumors about it undoubtedly create significant tension both among certain segments of the population and in society as a whole. And so, as you can see, even at the highest level, the Russian president addressed this issue, because the information really did spread extremely widely.

Obviously, there are opinion polls and there is analysis, but there is also a simple rule you can see in any personal chat group: if people you know start actively discussing a particular topic, then you know that topic is genuinely on people’s minds. I can say that this was discussed in every personal chat I am part of, and at every meeting I attended, someone asked a similar question. And it is clear that those who created and injected this fake news were relying on the idea that during the previous period, there was still a certain segment of people who became frightened and left, as well as the parents of those people, who were themselves under considerable stress. So, the objective pursued by our opponents is clear. I would identify this as one of the most prominent narratives we are observing.

– If it is possible to trace the source and, for example, make a list, a sort of tier list, of which countries carry out the most information attacks against Russia, what objectives are these countries pursuing?

– Ukraine is in first place, but this is fairly easy to explain. We are in a state of armed conflict, and today information warfare is part of the larger war. So, it would be strange if we were now talking about other countries dominating Ukraine in this regard. Ukraine has a separate unit, the Center for Information and Psychological Operations, or CIPsO, which is part of the regular armed forces and is classified as a military unit.

This is visible across many different issues. In other words, they get involved in any crisis-related topic and try to escalate it as much as possible and create additional tension around it. But at the same time, we understand that there are a number of countries that are also behaving quite aggressively and using specialized institutions to operate against us. First and foremost, this is Britain. This is a country that behaves quite aggressively in the information sphere. There are different methods. They have, so to speak, verified sources – media outlets and platforms that they support through various grant systems and through direct funding. There is also work involving AI, work targeting specific segments of the population, ranging from simple tactics in which certain issues are injected into the information space to more sophisticated operations.

But despite the fact that we are currently at a fairly acute stage of information confrontation, we should not discount ordinary people who often spread unreliable information without having any malicious intent. Again, this brings us back to the issue of cognitive awareness. Our task is to stop constantly saying that everything we see is somehow a product of our adversary. That is not the case. Fake news existed before. People tend, especially in situations when they feel uncertain or do not know the answers to questions that concern them, to come up with rather strange answers themselves, to put it politely, or to seek those answers in completely unverified sources. So here we need to work with the broader public so that people learn to verify information.

– So, what is needed is broad-based educational and explanatory work?

– Yes.

– Now let us talk about the association that you head. The Global Fact-Checking Network was established in 2025. Can you give us an interim assessment of this period? How has the nature of your activities, the scope of your tasks, and the scale of the network changed?

– First of all, I believe that the project has worked out overall. It is important to understand that this was initially a voluntary initiative. The project was created by us, by Russia’s News Agency TASS, and by the New Media Workshop. We created it amid the publicity surrounding our lawsuit against the FBI in the United States after we were accused of allegedly interfering in the US elections. And, to be completely honest, initially it was something of a PR move. But various industry participants from different countries showed interest, and today we have more than 125 journalists in the Association from 55 countries.

And every time at the forum (referring to the Dialogue about Fakes 4.0 forum – TASS), more and more speakers and participants from different countries attend. The total number of guests at the forum has already exceeded 2,000–3,000, including Russian participants, but a significant share still comes from different countries, including countries that are currently considered unfriendly, yet there are journalists and media professionals there who are willing to engage with us.

We have released a number of interesting and high-profile investigations, and we have developed a substantial educational program. Several memoranda have been adopted at major international events based on the GFCN Code of Responsible Fact-Checking. Some provisions of our Code were also included in the final statement of the 12th BRICS Communications Ministers’ Meeting at the recent summit in India. And today we have begun working quite closely with colleagues from China and Kazakhstan. A GFCN expert was in Kazakhstan during the elections as part of the CIS observation mission, and before that our representatives were in Venezuela. Again, we are invited to participate in various events, and it is important to understand that GFCN currently has no funding of any kind. In other words, we are essentially participants and members who have other, primary jobs, and for whom this is, as our opponents like to put it, a "guilty pleasure."

So, as a project created entirely on enthusiasm, I think the Network has exceeded my expectations in any case. On about five or six occasions already, the International Fact-Checking Network, a fact-checking association funded by the Poynter Institute, has mentioned in its articles that we are a lying Kremlin propaganda network. I consider that a great success. So, when I compare the resources invested with the results, I am very pleased with the work of the Network.

– We have already mentioned information adversaries. As allies, as I understand it, you have named China and Kazakhstan?

– There are actually many countries. We are currently integrating closely with the Organization of Asia-Pacific News Agencies (OANA), which is currently chaired by TASS Director General Andrey Kondrashov. So this includes Asia, the Pacific, Latin American countries, and CIS countries. Some show greater interest, others less. We are as open as possible here. We have an educational section on our website, which already contains more than 170 articles and videos covering various areas of fact-checking, media literacy, and OSINT tools (open-source intelligence research – TASS), all of which are available to users on the website. Our position here is quite open. We are not claiming ideological leadership; rather, we want to bring together people who are interested in this field. So, some countries show more active interest, and there are individual representatives of countries who are particularly active. But I would say that as this issue becomes increasingly relevant, interest will continue to grow.

– You have touched on the Network’s educational role. In your view, what qualities need to be cultivated among young journalists, fact-checkers, and researchers? What do you pay particular attention to, and what are you trying to develop?

– There is an expression: an inquisitive mind. I think that is the most important thing. I was personally the driving force behind launching this initiative, but I am not an OSINT specialist (a professional who collects, analyzes, and interprets information from publicly available sources – TASS) and I am not a fact-checker (a professional who specializes in verifying the accuracy of information – TASS) myself. What matters to me is creating a certain atmosphere for this "community" and giving it an opportunity to grow. And when I look at people who, in my view and in the view of my colleagues, have that kind of fact-checking talent, they are extremely inquisitive. They are meticulous, perhaps even somewhat distrustful at times, but I think people like that could work very well in law enforcement agencies.

I am exaggerating a little, of course, but you need to be appropriately skeptical. We are not talking about some kind of blind or irrational distrust. You need to start from the assumption that we live in a very difficult information environment filled with millions of unverified sources. At the same time, the internet now gives us the ability to verify an enormous amount of information without resorting to any closed or restricted verification methods. The ability to think critically on the one hand and to use these tools on the other, taken together, gives us an excellent synergy for helping these talented people grow and develop.

– From everything we have discussed, it already seems that fact-checking has ceased to be primarily a tool for journalists. Can we say that it has now become a distinct international area of cooperation? And what kind of global model for interaction would you perhaps propose?

– It is difficult for me to say what a global model of cooperation would look like, but I have thought, for example, about the fact that there are conventional rules governing warfare. If those rules are violated, there is a regulatory body where sanctions or consequences for such actions are considered. For example, is inducing a teenager to commit murder or arson as part of information warfare essentially the same thing as using cluster munitions in a conventional war? I believe it is. Because that goes beyond the bounds of information confrontation in the sense in which I see and understand it. And in my view, even if today we are talking about us and our adversaries with whom we are waging this information war, there still need to be certain rules. Unfortunately, as of today, there is no such framework for defining those rules. It would be quite difficult to establish it at the global level right now. We understand the geopolitical situation, especially if we were, so to speak, the ones initiating such an effort. But in my view, these rules need to emerge. And that is the next step.

But globally, despite all the popularity and hype surrounding fact-checking, it has still not become a fundamental part of journalism. And we need to understand that journalism itself has also undergone a transformation. As a graduate of the journalism faculty at Moscow State University, I can say that journalism today and journalism even 15 years ago are completely different fields, and today many major publications are facing the question of how they can continue to exist, because modern media consumption and the monetization of platforms that results from it seem not to provide for their presence on anything close to the same scale.

So, the question here is not how fact-checking will be incorporated into journalism; the broader question is what will happen to journalism itself in the coming years. And fact-checking, in my view, is not purely a journalistic field. At a basic everyday level, it is something that every adult today should possess at least minimal skills in for their own safety. At the professional level, it involves groups of ordinary people who work in the interests of private companies, in the interests of the state, and in their own interests, if they are investigators or people working in related fields.

– I will be completely candid: it is very interesting to listen to you, and it makes me want to delve deeper into these issues. On September 22, we have a major event coming up – the Dialogue about Fakes 4.0 forum, which will provide an opportunity to discuss all of this in greater detail.

– Yes, we will have presentations there, and we are very grateful to the Russian Foreign Ministry for supporting the forum throughout all these years. Without the Foreign Ministry, we certainly would not have been able to put together an event on this scale. And this year, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Viktorovich Lavrov will personally take part in the forum. We are very grateful to him for responding to our requests. And we are also grateful to Russian Foreign Ministry Spokeswoman Maria Vladimirovna Zakharova for her endless, consistent support.

– I do not like talking about any particular forum as being special, because then we somewhat diminish the value of the previous forums that came before it. In my view, the community is simply becoming larger, stronger, and broader. text: The Sahyog route also raises a serious constitutional concern. In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India, the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A because the blocking framework contained procedural safeguards, including notice, hearing and a reasoned order. text:
Question to X and Indian Authorities
Why did multiple X posts display the message “Due to local regulations, this content is restricted on X” when viewed from India?

Screenshots taken on 12 September 2026 show this message on multiple posts related to the BRICS Summit 2026, including posts by journalist Sidhant Sibal, Sarbananda Sonowal, and ANI concerning the summit, Cyril Ramaphosa’s arrival, and Xi Jinping’s arrival in Delhi.

For clarity, the screenshots document that the restriction message was displayed during a specific period on 12 September 2026. This post does not claim that the content remained restricted permanently, nor does it establish who initiated the restriction.

The screenshots by themselves do not establish whether the restriction resulted from an Indian government request, a court order, another legal process, X’s own compliance mechanism, or any other regulatory basis.

Therefore, I would like to ask @X @HMOIndia @PMOIndia @MIB_India @GoI_MeitY for clarification:

1• What specific law, rule, regulation, legal order, or other legal process formed the basis for restricting access to these posts in India during that period?

2• Was the restriction imposed following a request, direction, order, or other legal process from an Indian authority, or was it based on another mechanism?

3• If an Indian authority was involved, which authority issued or requested the restriction, subject to any applicable confidentiality requirements?

4• Was there a specific restriction order, written direction, court order, or other legal document relating to these posts?

5• If Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000 was the applicable legal basis, can the relevant provision and applicable procedure be identified?

6• If Section 69A was not the basis, what specific legal or regulatory mechanism applied?

7• What does X mean by “local regulations” in these particular notices? Does the phrase specifically refer to Indian law or to another applicable regulatory requirement?

Why this question matters

This post is not alleging wrongdoing, censorship, or improper conduct by any individual, government authority, X, or any other organisation.

The purpose is simply to seek clarity and transparency about the legal or regulatory basis for a temporary restriction that was visible to users in India.

Where legally permissible, users should be able to understand what legal basis applied, whether an authority requested or directed the restriction, what process was followed, and why the restriction applied to the specific posts during that particular period.

Argus Partners is pleased to announce that it successfully represented the liquidator of Aaj Ka Anand Papers Limited before the High Court of Judicature at Bombay in a writ petition challenging an order of the Disciplinary Committee of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India suspending his authorisation to act as an insolvency professional, along with the related show cause notice.

By its judgment dated August 25, 2026, the division bench of the High Court allowed the writ petitions and quashed the Disciplinary Committee's order, holding that the show cause notice and the resulting findings were vitiated by procedural irregularity and violation of principles of natural justice, including reliance on issues outside the scope of the underlying complaints and disregard of relevant material.

The judgment is significant since it reaffirms that a regulator must genuinely apply its mind to an investigation report before forming a prima facie opinion, rather than issuing a show cause notice on unconsidered material. It also underscores that a mere difference in interpretation of ambiguous regulatory provisions, absent any stakeholder grievance, cannot be equated with misconduct on the part of an insolvency professional. Finally, the Court took judicial notice of the disproportionate impact of the automatic suspension triggered upon mere issuance of a show cause notice under the Model Bye-Laws, calling on the Board to be more circumspect before invoking such proceedings against insolvency professionals.

The matter was argued by Rahul Dev (Partner) assisted by Arjun Amin (Senior Associate).

Abhi Na Kaho Demand Final Hai!
High Court ने liability merits पर decide नहीं की, मामला Appeal के लिए छोड़ा● ● ●

⭐ आज की बात
नमस्ते दोस्त!

मान लीजिए आपने GST Notice का detailed Reply दिया। फिर final Order आता है और आपको लगता है—“मेरी specific बात तो properly deal ही नहीं हुई!”
यही शिकायत लेकर दो Petitioners Delhi High Court पहुँचे। लेकिन जिस Order को challenge किया गया था, वह सिर्फ एक taxpayer का नहीं बल्कि 629 firms और individuals से जुड़ा common adjudication था।

● ● ●

⭐ मामला इतना बड़ा कैसे बना?
Department की investigation alleged fake-invoice network को लेकर थी। आरोप था कि actual supply के बिना invoices arrange किए गए और कई firms के जरिए ineligible 𝗜𝗧𝗖 avail कराया गया।

इसी chain में Petitioners के नाम common Order में Serial Nos. 616 और 618 पर थे।

Petitioners ने कहा—𝗦𝗖𝗡 में उनकी specific role साफ नहीं बताई गई, detailed Replies दिए गए, फिर भी individual defence properly consider नहीं हुई। उनका यह भी कहना था कि alleged dealing केवल M/s Sahuwala Exports Pvt. Ltd. के साथ एक single transaction तक सीमित थी।
अब असली सवाल था: क्या High Court सीधे Order quash करे, या पहले statutory 𝗔𝗽𝗽𝗲𝗮𝗹 का रास्ता अपनाया जाए?

● ● ●

⭐ Court के सामने turning point क्या था?
Court ने पहले यह देखा कि dispute decide करने के लिए किस तरह की examination चाहिए।

🔍 Replies duly consider हुए या नहीं?
🔍 Petitioners की precise role क्या थी?
🔍 Common adjudication में उनके transaction को अलग से कैसे देखा जाए?

Court ने माना कि ये disputed factual questions हैं। Impugned Order और उसकी typed copy paper book में Page 80 से 1,959 तक फैली थी।

इसलिए High Court ने factual re-examination में जाने के बजाय कहा कि Appellate Authority इन मुद्दों को appropriately examine कर सकती है।

● ● ●

⭐ इस Judgment का Crux Point
यहाँ crux सिर्फ “Reply ignore हुई” नहीं था।
निर्णायक बात यह थी कि उस grievance को decide करने के लिए detailed factual scrutiny चाहिए थी। Court ने यह नहीं कहा कि Reply ignore करना ठीक है; उसने कहा कि इस controversy का सही forum statutory Appeal है।

● ● ●

⭐ Judgment में किन Legal References का इस्तेमाल हुआ?

An extract from an article by Avay Shukla relevent to today's judgement on Swatantra  Bhardwaj bail-
'Jurisprudence in India today appears to be governed by four made-in-India/swadeshi doctrines which should be a blot on any justice system: fait accompli, sealed cover, ignore the science, and reward the criminal. Importantly, even constitutional challenges to the executive’s actions are kept on the backburner for so long (Article 370, CAA, SIR, Shiv Sena split) that by the time they are decided, it is impossible to turn back the clock and undo what the government of the day has already implemented on the ground.
The sealed cover has become the standard fallback option for denying full disclosure to civil society petitioners, or for not giving rebuttable reasons for a particular judgment (Rafale, Pegasus, Vantara, Hindenburg). Increasingly, this spectre of our swadeshi jurisprudence, like the executive, shows disdain and contempt for science, as in the case of stray dogs, Aravalli mountains, the Char Dham highway, and the Great Nicobar project. More trust is reposed on government-appointed committees and patently partisan ministries than on scientists, domain experts and specialised organisations working in the relevant field. Finally, this mutant form of justice also ensures that the criminal will be duly allowed to keep the proceeds of his crime (Ram Mandir theft, electoral bonds) even as his actions are declared irregular! A judicial paraprosdokian if ever there was one.'
Avay Shukla- Bumpy swadeshi model of justice.
The Tribune 19 July 2026

फैसला करो, Forward नहीं
Appellate Authority को खुद merits पर decide करना होगा — file वापस घुमाना allowed नहीं.

● ● ●

⭐ आज की बात
नमस्ते दोस्त!

GST Appeal में documents देने के बाद taxpayer की उम्मीद होती है कि Appellate Authority अब final फैसला देगी।
K A Traders के मामले में file verification के लिए फिर Original Adjudicating Authority की तरफ लौट गई।

यहीं सवाल उठा: क्या First Appellate Authority final decision देने के बजाय matter वापस भेज सकती है?

● ● ●

⭐ कहानी कहाँ से शुरू हुई?
2017 से 2022 के Audit के बाद K A Traders पर GST demand बनी। First Appeal reject होने के बाद taxpayer ने rectification application के साथ further documents दिए।

JC (Appeals) ने ₹1,18,889 की demand drop कर दी। लेकिन बाकी ₹4,23,345 पर खुद final conclusion देने के बजाय Original Authority से कहा—documents और tax calculation verify करो; सही पाए जाएँ तो demand उतनी सीमा तक delete कर दो।

यानी Appeal का फैसला वहीं पूरा नहीं हुआ, file फिर नीचे चली गई।

● ● ●

⭐ यहीं Department ने सवाल उठाया
Department ने कहा 𝗦𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝟭𝟬𝟳(𝟭𝟭) ऐसा remand करने की power नहीं देता।

Taxpayer ने कहा relevant documents Appellate Authority के सामने थे और Revenue Appeal पर ₹20 lakh monetary-limit objection भी उठाया।

GSTAT के सामने मुद्दा था—Appellate Authority की jurisdiction कहाँ तक है?

● ● ●

⭐ GSTAT ने क्या देखा?
🔍 Tribunal ने कहा: documents मंगाने हों, records देखने हों, figures verify करने हों या further inquiry करनी हो—Appellate Authority यह सब कर सकती है।

लेकिन inquiry के बाद final decision भी उसे ही देना होगा।

तीन रास्ते हैं—𝗰𝗼𝗻𝗳𝗶𝗿𝗺, 𝗺𝗼𝗱𝗶𝗳𝘆 या 𝗮𝗻𝗻𝘂𝗹।

“Original Officer verify करे, फिर demand decide करे” कहना substance में remand है—और Section 107(11) First Appellate Authority को ऐसा refer-back करने से रोकता है।

● ● ●

⭐ इस Judgment का Crux Point
Turning point ₹4,23,345 की demand का merits नहीं था।

असल बात यह थी कि First Appellate Authority अपनी appellate responsibility Original Authority को वापस नहीं सौंप सकती।

Verification या further inquiry चाहिए? खुद करिए। फिर reasoned final order भी खुद दीजिए।

● ● ●

⭐ Judgment में किन Legal References का इस्तेमाल हुआ?

It wasn’t.

The reported structure is also important: roughly $1.5 billion is being discussed as a bridge facility, while another roughly $1 billion would come through a five-year loan. The report says the financing is being split across different pools of offshore and domestic liquidity.

So before asking “what’s cooking?”, perhaps read beyond the headline.

There is no reported loan waiver here.

There is no reported default here.

There is no reported government bailout here.

There is a proposed refinancing exercise.

Even the RBI framework explicitly permits refinancing of eligible external commercial borrowings subject to conditions such as compliance with the applicable framework, lower all-in cost and maturity requirements. 1

If there is evidence of political intervention, preferential lending or a distressed restructuring, put that evidence on the table.

Merely discovering that refinancing involves using new financing to retire existing debt is not an exposé. It is the definition of the transaction.

INDIA CRACKS DOWN ON AI & DEEP FAKE. BIG TECH PUT ON NOTCE

1. What has actually changed?

The Modi government amended the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021 on 10 February 2026 specifically to deal with synthetically generated information and deepfakes.
The framework covers deceptive AI-generated audio, visual and audio-visual material.
The idea is no longer simply: remove illegal content after somebody complains.

Platforms are now being pushed towards:
identification
labelling
metadata
verification
automated detection
rapid takedown
and greater accountability for allowing unlawful AI content to spread.

2. AI CONTENT HAS TO BE IDENTIFIABLE
This is probably the biggest structural change.
AI-generated/synthetically altered material covered by the rules has to be clearly identifiable as synthetic.
Platforms/services enabling generation or alteration of such content must ensure appropriate labels or traceable identifiers/metadata.
The objective is simple:
REAL CONTENT ≠ AI CONTENT
The viewer should not have to conduct a forensic investigation to figure out whether something was artificially generated.
Important nuance

Don't say “every piece of text written using AI anywhere on the internet must carry a label.”

MeitY's FAQ clarifies that the operative 2026 SGI definition primarily targets audio, visual and audio-visual information, not ordinary AI-generated written text.
A more accurate line for your video is:
“India has mandated identification and labelling requirements for covered AI-generated synthetic media, particularly deepfake audio, images and video.”

3. THE BIG NUMBER: 36 HOURS → 3 HOURS

Previously, once an intermediary received legally valid knowledge of unlawful material through the prescribed government/court process, the compliance window could be 36 hours.

That has now been cut to:

3 HOURS

That is a 91.7% reduction in response time.

So something capable of going viral nationally during an election, riot, communal incident, stock-market panic or national-security crisis can no longer theoretically remain online for a day and a half after a valid takedown direction.

The platform has only hours.

4. AND SOME COMPLAINT WINDOWS ARE EVEN SHORTER

The government says timelines for grievance redressal have also been compressed.

According to the PIB explanation:
certain complaints earlier subject to 72 hours can now require action within 36 hours

particularly sensitive categories that earlier had a 24-hour timeline can now require action within 2 hours

This specifically matters for areas such as:

impersonation

intimate imagery

nudity

deepfake abuse

other highly sensitive material.

5. BIG TECH CAN'T JUST WAIT FOR A COMPLAINT

This is another major change.

The government says intermediaries must deploy reasonable and appropriate technical measures, including automated tools or other mechanisms, against unlawful synthetically generated content.
That means platforms are increasingly being pushed from:
REACTIVE MODERATION
to
PROACTIVE DETECTION
For Significant Social Media Intermediaries, the framework explicitly envisages technical measures to identify prohibited content, including certain forms of:

rape-related material

child sexual abuse material

repeat prohibited content

unlawful synthetic content.

6. USERS MAY HAVE TO DECLARE AI CONTENT

The synthetic-media framework also places responsibility upstream.

Major platforms can be required to ask users uploading covered content whether it is synthetically generated and then use technical systems to check that declaration.

So theoretically:
User uploads video →
declares AI/not AI →
platform checks →
synthetic material gets labelled.

The earlier draft framework explicitly envisaged this declaration + technical-verification model.

7. WHY THE METADATA PART MATTERS

A visible watermark can be:

cropped,
blurred,
edited,
screen-recorded,

reposted.

Metadata/identifiers create another layer of traceability.

The government's objective is therefore not merely:

“PUT AI GENERATED IN THE CAPTION.”
It is building a system where synthetic content can carry technological indicators allowing platforms to recognise what it is.
That becomes especially useful once the same manipulated video is downloaded and re-uploaded across multiple platforms.
8. THE RULES TARGET DEEPFAKE IMPERSONATION DIRECTLY
Existing IT Rules already prohibit users from publishing material that:

impersonates another person

misleads users about the origin of a message

knowingly spreads patently false or misleading information

threatens public order

violates another applicable law.

AI does not create an exemption.

If AI is being used for impersonation, fraud, defamatory fabrication or other unlawful activity, existing criminal and cyber provisions can also apply.

9. BNS CAN ALSO COME INTO PLAY
The PIB release specifically points towards provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita.
Depending upon what the deepfake is being used for, authorities could examine provisions relating to:
Section 319 — cheating by personation
Section 336 — forgery

Section 353 — false information/rumours capable of causing public mischief or fear

Section 111 — organised crime, where the factual circumstances justify it.

So there isn't necessarily a standalone offence called simply:

“making a deepfake.”

The legal consequence depends heavily upon what the deepfake does.

10. CHILD SEXUAL ABUSE DEEPFAKES GET SPECIAL ATTENTION
This is perhaps the least discussed but most important provision.
The amended framework explicitly covers harmful AI-generated material involving:
child sexual exploitation

non-consensual intimate imagery

impersonation

other prohibited synthetic material.

Platforms are expected to prevent such content and act rapidly when detected.

11. SOCIAL-MEDIA GIANTS HAVE EXTRA DUTIES

Platforms classified as Significant Social Media Intermediaries, broadly those crossing the prescribed Indian user threshold, face additional compliance obligations.

These include mechanisms involving:
automated detection
grievance officers
compliance officers

local points of contact

India-based compliance structures

periodic compliance reports

appeals processes

originator tracing in specified circumstances for messaging services.
So the rules are aimed not only at the person creating the deepfake.
They put a major compliance burden on the distribution network itself.
12. THE REAL STICK: SAFE HARBOUR
This is where it becomes serious for Meta, X, Google, Telegram and other intermediaries.
Section 79 of the IT Act provides intermediaries conditional protection from liability for third-party content.
But that protection depends upon complying with the law and prescribed due diligence.
The PIB release reiterates that failure to observe obligations under the IT Rules can result in the intermediary losing its Section 79 exemption, after which liability can arise under applicable law.

That makes the real equation:

Comply with due diligence → retain intermediary protection

Ignore statutory obligations → safe-harbour protection can be jeopardised

That is far more powerful than merely issuing a fine.

13. GOVERNMENT HAS BUILT A TAKEDOWN PIPELINE

There is now an increasingly integrated enforcement architecture:

Grievance Appellate Committees — GACs

Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre — I4C

SAHYOG Portal

National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal

police/cybercrime units

authorised State and Central Government agencies.

The SAHYOG system in particular enables centralised electronic communication of lawful content-removal notices to intermediaries.

14. INDIA IS ALSO BUILDING ITS OWN DEEPFAKE-DETECTION TECHNOLOGY

Under the IndiaAI Mission's Safe & Trusted AI pillar, government-backed work includes indigenous detection and governance technologies.
PIB identifies projects including:
Saakshya — multi-agent deepfake-detection framework developed by IIT Jodhpur and IIT Madras
AI Vishleshak — audio-visual forgery detection
IIT Kharagpur work on real-time voice deepfake detection.

So this is not purely a legal crackdown.

It is simultaneously a:

LEGAL + PLATFORM + TECHNOLOGICAL framework.

15. WHY THIS IS HAPPENING NOW

Generative AI has destroyed the old assumption that:
“Seeing is believing.”
Today one person can manufacture:

a politician announcing something he never said

a CEO apparently moving a stock

an Army officer issuing a fake warning

communal speeches

celebrity pornography

fake financial endorsements

fabricated battlefield footage

false evidence of violence
within minutes.
And the fake can reach millions before conventional fact-checking catches up.
Therefore the Indian approach is increasingly:
IDENTIFY → LABEL → DETECT → TRACE → REMOVE → PROSECUTE
rather than merely:
WAIT → RECEIVE COMPLAINT → INVESTIGATE.
THE BIG STORY FOR YOUR VIDEO

The headline isn't simply:

“Deepfakes must carry labels.”

The bigger story is that India is trying to change where responsibility lies.

Earlier, platforms could largely argue:

A user uploaded it; we are merely the intermediary.

The regulatory direction is increasingly:

If you operate the technology that generates, distributes or algorithmically amplifies synthetic content in India, you have duties to identify it, label it and respond rapidly when it becomes unlawful.

HOPE THAT HELPS

The Sacred and the Toxic: Constitutional Nihilism and the Death of the Yamuna

This video is ex facie documentary evidence of constitutional failure. The Yamuna, reduced to a toxic froth, stands as a mockery of Article 21. The Supreme Court in M.C. Mehta unequivocally held that the right to a clean environment is intrinsic to the right to life. Yet, for the women bathing in this poisonous lather, that fundamental right is a dead letter.

The legal record is damning. NGT penalties against the Delhi Jal Board and MCD are routinely stayed. The "Polluter Pays" principle remains a mere slogan. The Supreme Court’s suo motu cognizance of Yamuna pollution was abandoned, delegating the crisis to the NGT—a classic instance of judicial abdication. BOD levels at ITO bridge stand at 25 mg/l against a safe limit of 3 mg/l. This is not a natural calamity; it is a willful, man-made tragedy.

We are constrained to draw a stark parallel: the State’s investigative machinery awakens with alacrity when unaccounted cash is found in a minister's house. But when thousands of litres of industrial poison flow into the Yamuna daily, why is no one held accountable?

Articles 48A and 51A(g) impose a binding constitutional duty on the State and citizens to protect the environment. A duty without a sanction is a legal fiction.

We demand immediate contempt proceedings against the senior officials of the Delhi Jal Board and MCD for willful disobedience of NGT orders. We demand the strict, uncompromising enforcement of the "Polluter Pays" principle. The Constitution does not permit the State to drown its citizens in poison while hiding behind procedural delays.

The Yamuna is dying. The law must intervene, or it stands indicted alongside the State.

By NK Goswami,Advocate,Supreme Court of India

Eyes on the Road: Judicial Fiat Alone Cannot Prevent Traffic Fatalities

Introduction

India’s road-safety crisis reflects not merely individual negligence but a deeper systems failure, demanding a transition from punitive enforcement towards a Safe System approach that anticipates human error.

Main Facts

India has nearly 1% of the global vehicle fleet but around 11% of road fatalities.

In 2024, two-wheeler riders constituted 46.2% and pedestrians 20.6% of road deaths.

Non-use of helmets, seat belts and child restraints aggravates mortality; post-crash investigations reveal ejection and secondary collisions.

The Motor Vehicles (Amendment) Act, 2019 introduced mechanisms for improving road safety, but outcomes remain inadequate.

Speeding remains a dominant behavioural factor associated with fatalities.

The Supreme Court has asked the Centre to consider measures for wider adoption of safety practices.

Challenges

1. Weak enforcement: Chronic shortages of traffic personnel undermine compliance.

2. Unsafe infrastructure: Accident-prone road designs magnify human errors.

3. High-risk mobility: Pedestrians and two-wheeler users remain disproportionately exposed.

4. Institutional fragmentation: Road safety involves multiple agencies without sufficiently integrated action.

5. Limited safety culture: Risky behaviour often lacks sustained social deterrence.

Constructive Criticism

Judicial intervention can catalyse accountability, but judicial fiat cannot substitute for administrative capacity. Excessive emphasis on helmets and seat belts addresses only a fraction of fatalities. The deeper challenge is to redesign the transport ecosystem so that inevitable human mistakes do not become fatal.

Way Forward

Adopt the Safe System approach through:

Safer road engineering and correction of black spots.

Speed management through design and technology.

Better pedestrian infrastructure and protection of vulnerable users.

Stronger traffic policing and automated enforcement.

Mandatory tamper-proof seat-belt reminders and safer vehicle standards.

Faster trauma care and post-crash response.

Sustained public campaigns for behavioural change.

Highlighted Keywords

Safe System | Human Error | Vulnerable Road Users | Speed Management | Road Engineering | Black Spots | Traffic Enforcement | Trauma Care | Behavioural Change

Conclusion

Road safety must evolve from “blame the driver” to “design the system”—making roads, vehicles, enforcement and emergency care collectively resilient to human fallibility.

Statement : The blocking of BitChat's code on GitHub is unconstitutional and authoritarian. 

New Delhi, 24 July 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the order issued by the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), Ministry of Home Affairs, directing GitHub to remove the code repositories of BitChat. 

The order, Notice No. 11072601011432, was issued at 11:16 pm on 23 July 2026 under Section 79(3)(b) of the Information Technology Act, 2000 read with Rule 3(1)(d) of the IT Rules, 2021. The order directs GitHub to disable access to three repositories, including the Android application and its release files, within three hours. It threatens the platform with loss of safe harbour and criminal prosecution. No copy was published by the Government of India. The public learnt of it from a post by @jack, whose team develops BitChat. Censorship in India now comes to light through disclosure by the censored.

Since 17 July 2026, the Ministry of Home Affairs has suspended mobile internet around Jantar Mantar as per public reports about five times, most recently within a 1.5 kilometre radius from 4 pm until midnight on 23 July. That radius takes in Janpath and parts of Connaught Place. Reports describe signal jammers at the protest site and people walking two kilometres before their phones work. Inside that zone a student separated from her group during a detention drive cannot send a message to say where she is. Thousands of students and young people have camped at Jantar Mantar since June, seeking accountability for examination irregularities. Permission for their march to Parliament was refused. Metro stations were shut and also internet connectivity has been blocked.

BitChat is an open source application built for exactly this situation. It passes messages from phone to phone over Bluetooth, without mobile networks or a central server. It is striking that the order does not identify a single unlawful message. It objects to what BitChat is. In its own words, the application is dangerous because it enables communication "even during network restrictions" and can "circumvent lawful restrictions" during "internet shutdowns". Hence, the government's objection is that citizens can speak to one another while it has switched the internet off. 

The order is illegal on at least four grounds. 

1. Section 79(3)(b) is not a blocking power. In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, the Supreme Court read down the provision. Intermediaries may be required to act only on a court order, or a government notification confined to the grounds under Article 19(2) of the Constitution. Blocking is governed exclusively by Section 69A and the Blocking Rules, 2009, which require a hearing and reasons recorded in writing, subject to review. Directions issued under Section 79(3)(b), Rule 3(1)(d) and the Sahyog Portal evade these safeguards, and constitutional challenges to this parallel regime are pending before High Courts. 

2. The reasons in the order are circular. The order asserts that the repositories contain "information which is prohibited under any law" without naming any such information, and rests on what the application is "capable of" enabling. Anticipated misuse of a communications tool is not a lawful basis to prohibit the tool. By this logic a telephone exchange could be sealed. 

3. The order cites Section 43 of the IT Act, a civil compensation provision, alongside conspiracy and abetment offences under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, against a platform that hosts code. 

4. A three hour deadline issued close to midnight forecloses legal assessment and recourse, and fails the proportionality standard in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) 3 SCC 637.

The order also fails on its own terms as deleting a repository does not delete the application from any phone that carries it, and the mesh keeps functioning without servers. What the takedown actually prevents is scrutiny of the underlying code.

IFF demands that the Government of India:

1. Withdraw Notice No. 11072601011432 dated 23 July 2026 issued to GitHub.
2. Publish every takedown direction issued under Section 79(3)(b), Rule 3(1)(d) and the Sahyog Portal, with the reasons recorded for each.
3. Restore full connectivity around Jantar Mantar, publish all suspension orders, and disclose the legal authority for the deployment of jammers.

We stand with the developers and the young protesters whose speech this order seeks to silence.
